speechtext:
I fear, Mr. Speaker, that the opening words of the minister to the effect that he had not much to say about this act at this time are both ominous and disappointing. I had hoped that he would have a great deal to tell us about much wider extensions that were being granted to the recipients of the war veterans' allowance than those to which he has referred this evening. It is true that the benefits of the act are now to be extended to those men who served in forces other than the Canadian forces in world war I, who have reached advancing years and who have lived in this country for a period of not less than twenty years. When one realizes that the war of 1914 started over thirty-five years ago and that some of the men who will now

War Veterans Allowance Act reap the benefits by this extension oi the allowance will have lived in Canada for thirty years, it seems a little bit ironical that the minister should have referred to implementing the provisions of this bill, when passed, with the utmost dispatch. Thirty-five years is rather a long time to wait to begin to show such determination to lose no greater time.
Not only have organized bodies of the veterans been pressing for this extension over a great many years -but resolutions have been sent forward to this house, to the committee on veterans affairs when it was sitting, and to individual members from the Legion, from the Army and Navy Veterans and from other organized bodies of veterans urging that those men who had served alongside the Canadian forces in an actual theatre of war and had then immigrated to this country should be given the same benefits as the Canadian soldiers, who were their comrades, sharing the same hardships, occupying the same trenches, who were serving at sea together and who were taking part in the air operations of the first war.
Hon. members on this side of the house must be pleased that the extension of this allowance is being granted to the men who served with us in the other forces of the empire. I think it will be recalled that time and time again members on this side of the house have been urging this extension. The delay has been long. Thirty-five years is a long time. Many of the men who emigrated, perhaps in the twenties, and have been out here living in this country, are men who have in every sense of the word proved themselves to be fine citizens of Canada, who have contributed to the economic welfare of this country, who have paid their taxes regularly, who have raised their families and whose sons and daughters fought in the second world war with the Canadian forces. They have had a long time to wait.
Unfortunately, many of those men have passed on to the great beyond, leaving behind them widows and in some cases orphans. It seems but poor gratitude that the government should overlook those widows who would have been in receipt of this allowance had their husbands lived until this date. But unfortunately their husbands have passed on and those widows are not only in the straitened circumstances that occur today but are deprived of an allowance which would have been their due had their husbands lived until now. I cannot understand how the minister can have overlooked those widows of the imperial soldiers, women who have lived in this country for twenty years, women 
whose husbands, had they lived, would have been entitled to this allowance and now are not to have the benefits extended to them. I hope that before the minister introduces his bill, he will take into consideration the pleas which are being made by organized bodies of veterans all over the country, and by me in the remarks that I am now making, and that when this bill is presented a further amendment will be brought in so that it will include the widows of the ex-imperial soldiers, widows who have lived in this country for twenty years and whose husbands would have been in receipt of this allowance had they lived until this date. Many recommendations have been made along those lines. I have received a great many communications, not only from my own constituency but from other parts of Canada. I am going to put on the record one such telegram as indicative of the feeling across the country on this particular point. I quote a telegram that I have received since the Easter recess from the legion in my home city of Nanaimo. It reads:
Would ask your immediate support to have proposed amendment to War Veterans Allowance Act extending benefits of act to imperial veterans further amended before it goes to the House of Commons to provide the benefits of the act to widows of imperial veterans with twenty years residence in Canada but whose husbands died before completing twenty years' residence in Canada.
It is signed by the secretary of the legion. It is typical of many such messages that I have received. The same remarks will apply to the reference to the War Veterans Allowance Act for mothers. Soldiers are entitled to certain benefits under part II of the act exactly the same as the widows are entitled to certain benefits under part II of the act. I would ask the minister to revise the bill which will be brought into the house shortly so that the benefits of the act may be extended to those further groups.
Then again I cannot help feeling that this might have been an opportunity to raise the basic rate of the war veterans' allowance. At the moment the basic rate is less than that paid to the old age pensioners in the province of British Columbia and in other provinces. They may get some other small benefits which perhaps old age pensioners do not get, but the-fact remains that the basic rate is lower than that of the old age pensioners. It is not a condition about which the returned men of this country feel happy, because they believe that their old comrades should have just as good protection as that which is meted out to the aged citizens who did not see service. After all, this War Veterans Allowance Act was introduced to provide the equivalent of an old age pension to soldiers, sailors and airmen who had seen service in an actual

theatre of war and who, because of their service, were presumed to have prematurely aged.
I know these allowances have been increased since they were first authorized, but since the increase was last made the cost of living has gone up. Figures quoted in the house earlier this week indicated that the index figure of the cost of living was now higher than it had ever been before in Canada; that it had risen to 163-7. That is only an indication of how imperative it is to try and assist the aged veterans of world war I.
I know an act was passed a year ago under which additional assistance might be given to the extent of $10 a month in regular payments. But the number of veterans who have received that additional payment in British Columbia is only a very small percentage of the actual recipients of the war veterans' allowance. There are, or there were in February of this year, 6,390 recipients of war veterans' allowance in British Columbia, but only 880 were receiving the additional $10 a month regular payment. I am sure that the experience we have gained in the past year, through the payment of this additional assistance, has borne out the fact in British Columbia that that extra assistance does not meet the situation as it exists.
Again, branches of the legion have been recommending an increase in the basic allowance, and I had hoped-and I still hope-that the minister would see fit to include in the bill, which he will be presenting when this resolution is passed, an additional amendment to authorize an increase in that basic allowance.
Many other recommendations have been made by the Legion that other groups should be included. I am not going to enumerate all of them. I know the minister has received the resolutions which were passed by the Legion last December urging further extensions of these allowances.
Regarding the second principle involved in this resolution, namely, the decentralization of the administration, on the whole the administration has been working satisfactorily; and I think the minister is justified in complimenting his deputy minister and the other officials who have been responsible for the administration of the war veterans' allowances. Whether it is going to be advantageous to decentralize that administration at the present time is perhaps debatable. Anyway, a good deal of further information is required on that subject before hon. members are able to make a firm decision on the matter. Therefore, because of the additional extensions which have been recommended, the uncertainty as to the application of the principle
War Veterans Allowance Act of decentralization, I sincerely hope that the minister will follow the example of his colleagues in other departments and when the bill which he will introduce, based on this resolution, is brought before the house and given second reading, he will refer it to a special committee on veterans affairs.
A special committee on veterans affairs has been asked for by organized groups of veterans for a long time. It has been a disappointment to them that such a committee has not been set up during the last two sessions of parliament. While it might not be the minister's intention to set up a committee similar to that which was in operation previously, I do hope that a committee will be set up so that representatives from the organized groups of veterans may have an opportunity of coming before a committee of members of parliament to give firsthand evidence as to why they feel that further extensions of this allowance are so necessary to meet the situation facing the aged veterans of this country today.

Mr. Speaker, those of us in this group are extremely pleased to see this legislation brought down at the present time. We believe however that this should have been done a good many years ago. Many veterans who have been recipients of the allowance under the act have been waiting for twenty-five or thirty years, as has been pointed out by previous speakers. That is a long time for anyone to wait for something to which he has been entitled all along.
Many of these men have been in Canada for thirty years and have served the country in the role of citizens. Their work in Canada alone should merit recognition, even without the war service they had given prior to coming to Canada.
I would strongly urge that when drawing up the bill the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) consider seriously making it retroactive for at least a year, in recognition of the fact that the government has been too tardy in bringing down the legislation.
The suggestion to decentralize, so as to bring the administration of the act within the control of the eighteen boards across Canada, will result, we believe, in a great saving of time, and bring the authority closer to the applicants. It will make the investigation of cases much more convenient and cause them to go through with a minimum of effort and waste of time.
As I said before, we firmly support the bill, so far as it goes. We do believe however that it should go much further. The present basic allowance is a mere pittance, when one considers the increase in the cost of

living, and especially after consideration of the increased cost of the essentials required for the bare level of existence many of these veterans are forced to put up with. We submit that the basic allowance should be increased, as has been urged by the two previous speakers. This should be increased to the rate recommended in the submissions made by veterans' organizations across Canada, that is, to $50 for the single veteran and $85 for the married veteran. The present allowance of $40.41 for the single and $70.83 for the married veteran is entirely insufficient. As a matter of fact, it is less than the old age pension paid in some of the provinces. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) referred to the old age pension paid in British Columbia and the same remarks are applicable to my own province of Alberta. These amounts are being paid for war services rendered to Canada and that payment should be adequate.
We join with hon. members who have spoken already in urging that a clause be inserted in the bill to take care, not only of widows of imperial veterans but of widows of our own Canadian veterans. It is a shame that a woman should be penalized because her husband dies. During the years that the veteran has suffered because of his war service his wife has shared in those inconveniences and she should be entitled to the same consideration given to the veteran.
There should also be a clause in the bill to provide medical and hospital care for wives, widows and dependents of these veterans. Some of the provinces provide for nospitalization and medical care for those in receipt of old age pensions. It is the right of every veteran, not only as a veteran but as a pioneer citizen, to expect the same kind of treatment.
We join with other speakers in urging the setting up of a special veterans affairs committee so that the leaders of the various service organizations across Canada can give their views on the various matters affecting veterans legislation. I do not think the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) can be blamed for not setting up this committee. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution forecasts two changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act. One will make members of allied forces who served in the first war and have been living in Canada for twenty years eligible for these benefits. The other change is in connection with the administration of the act.
With respect to the first change, I should hope there would be no disagreement in this house. In fact to me it is a great tragedy that the imperial and other allied veterans should have had to wait so long to become eligible for the war veterans' allowance. I need only point out that thousands of those


veterans served in the Canadian forces in the second war. That service did not enable them to qualify for the war veterans' allowance, however, because they were nearly all in the veterans' guard and as we all know very few of the veterans' guard were allowed to go overseas. In addition many of these allied veterans had sons serving with our sons in the Canadian forces during the recent war. Giving them entitlement to the war veterans' allowance is a step long overdue.
In connection with this proposal I urge the minister to make the payments retroactive, at least to the date the announcement was made in this house that the imperials would be given entitlement. His parliamentary assistant made that announcement on December 10 of last year, the last day of the second session of 1949, and at that time I asked whether it would not be possible to have payments made retroactive to that date. I urge the minister to have his legislation provide that payments shall begin as of December 10, 1949, at least.
Then I hope there is no doubt that those veterans who served in the imperial forces during the South African war will be eligible for the allowance after these amendments are made. The minister nods his head. I am very glad to learn that such is to be the case. Another suggestion that has been made by each of the preceding speakers, and with which I agree, is that the widows of veterans who have died should be made eligible. There seems to be an impression abroad that the act is not wide enough to cover those widows. When we make this change, let us do it right and provide eligibility for the widows of these veterans. I do not think anyone in the house would be against extending the act to provide for them.
With regard to the amount of the war veterans' allowance, surely there can be no doubt that the amounts paid are too low. That, of course, is because of the present cost of living. Only a year or two ago the minister's department made a survey across Canada, which disclosed that the recipients of the war veterans' allowance were not getting enough to live on. As a result we had a special vote last year setting up what is known as the war veterans' assistance fund. That survey proved conclusively what some of us have been trying to tell the government for a long time; that is, that the war veterans' allowance is insufficient to enable these men and their wives to carry on. This year the position is even worse, and that assistance fund is to be increased from $500,000 to $750,000, though only approximately ten per

cent of those in receipt of the war veterans' allowance have been able to qualify for this assistance.
That whole picture shows conclusively that the allowance should be increased. At the present time it is $40.41 a month for a single veteran and $70.83 for a married man. In British Columbia a single old age pensioner gets $50 a month, and the wife of a married pensioner can also get $50 a month if she is seventy years of age. In addition they are given free hospitalization and free medical and dental care. We have a case of an old age pensioner who served in the German army in the first war and he and his wife are now drawing $100 a month-and I am not quarrelling with that, since under the law they have a perfect right to it-and within a door or two of where they live there is a veteran who served in the Canadian forces, but he and his wife get only $70.83. That is an intolerable situation. The war veterans' allowance should be increased at least to the amount of the old age pension. I know that everyone in British Columbia is in favour of a change being made which would bring the allowance up to the amount paid by way of old age pension.
Before I continue, I should like to say a word about this war veterans' assistance fund. I should like to read a paragraph or two from an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Sun on November 12, 1949. The newspaper offices are close to Victory square in Vancouver, in which there is a monument to our dead of the first war. These newspapermen had witnessed the services held there the day before, November 11, and this editorial appeared on the following day. It is entitled "Burnt Out and Burned up". I wish to quote certain paragraphs, which I think neatly sum up this situation. In referring to the burnt out veterans, it says:
They are today in a worse position than old age pensioners. Beth are supported from public funds. Why in the name of all that is reasonable should those who made special sacrifices for their country be subsequently penalized? Surely the least that could be done is set the W.V.A. rate at a figure equal to the O.A.P., even if the former may qualify before age seventy.
The article goes on to list the differences in amounts received by the veteran and the recipients of the old age pension. Then it says:
True, Ottawa at the last session of parliament started a special emergency fund for W.V.A. pur-coses, from which district authorities might make idditional grants in aid in cases of extreme destitu-;ion. Some W.V.A. recipients have benefited under his provision. But extra allowances are subject o a periodical means test, and the funds are limited -which means more penny-pinching by D.V.A. cfficials seeking to help. And winter at hand means 'urther hardship for many.

War Veterans Allowance Act
Some of the wives of older veterans are voluntarily abandoning their $30 W.V.A. allowance to claim old age pension. Obviously, however, only a few of them are old enough to do so.
If the minister checks up, I believe he will find that his own officers are advising veterans who are seventy years of age or over to go off the war veterans' allowance, and get on the old age pension. It is a tragedy that such should be the case, because the veteran is a direct charge on the dominion government, and should certainly receive as much as those people who are at least partially looked after by the provincial government.
I continue reading from the editorial:
Lest we forget! One can understand the pathetic figures who bravely attended remembrance day services yesterday, trying to keep heads high despite anxious hearts. One can forgive bitterness, too.
But one cannot forgive the heartlessness of politicians. A remedy could still be effected this session, and should be effected.
Mr. Speaker, this editorial appeared in the leading Liberal paper in British Columbia.
Public opinion would back the insistent demands of veterans organizations that Ottawa no longer shirk its duty.
Ottawa is shirking its duty as long as it refuses to raise these war veterans' allowances to an amount at least equal to the old age pension.
As for the special assistance, I think it helps out; but it should not be used as a substitute for a proper increase in the allowance itself. The assistance fund should be used for the odd case where there are special conditions, but most of the veterans who are now receiving that assistance would have their needs met if the war veterans' allowance were set at an appropriate figure. The member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has made some reference to the form that has to be filled out by the applicant for special assistance. Of course, there is a second means test, and the veteran has to go through that humiliation. The dominion investigator has to find out such things as this: Entitlement to assistance from other sources, for example, social assistance, mothers' allowance, old age pensions, family allowance, medical and hospital care. No veteran in Canada should be forced to depend on social assistance in a province; he should be cared for by the dominion.
There is another weakness in this fund, in that it is only provided by annual grant of parliament. There is no legislation behind it. The grant is made for one year and must be renewed year after year. The veteran does not know whether he is going to receive it the next year. There is nothing final about it. It should be provided by way of legislation rather than under an annual vote.
!742	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act So much for the amount of the war veterans' allowance; now let me say a word about the administration of the act. This proposal to decentralize the administration is made because of inefficiency in the administration of the act. Let there be no mistake about that. I am not quarrelling with the change, because I think it is a proper one, but I do not think this act has been administered as it should have been. I realize that the men on the war veterans' allowance board have a difficult job. I am not saying they are trying to do anything but their best, but from my own experience I am convinced the time has come to check the administration of this act, and check it carefully.
The difficulties may be overcome by decentralization, by giving more power to the men out in Vancouver, in Calgary or in Winnipeg, who are in direct contact with the veteran.
I believe they can get a clearer picture of the needs of the veteran than any board here in Ottawa. I believe also that they can get much quicker action. I am, therefore, in favour of decentralization.
Here are some of the ways in which administration has been, in my opinion, faulty. When the veterans affairs committee sat, I think it was in 1948, there was a change in the provision for casual earnings. Before that time casual earnings had been limited to a certain amount. The members of that committee felt that there should be a change; that the veteran should be allowed to get whatever casual earnings he could. Eventually the act was changed accordingly, and I think that was a proper change. Yet I have had
a case___I will give the minister these cases
later__in which a veteran was unable to do
any work; his wife was going out doing housework She was in poor health herself, and when she went to do this housework she occasionally suffered a break-down owing to her poor health. The war veterans' allowance board decided that, because she was earning a little bit of money doing domestic work, these were regular earnings and her husband's allowance was cut accordingly. I believe there was a claim for overpayment.
This trouble was partially the fault of the investigator because he did not talk to the wife herself. He spoke to the lady for whom she worked, and came back with the story that she worked two regular days a week. That was considered to be regular earnings and took the veteran away from the provision for casual earnings, with the results I have already indicated. The facts, however, were that the woman did not work any steady days a week and that for periods of time she had been unable to work at all. If there ever was a case in which earnings
[K'r. Green.]

were casual, this was such a case. Yet that veteran had his allowance cut. There should be a benefit of the doubt given to these recipients of war veterans' allowance just as there is under the Pension Act. I do not believe there is one member of this house who served on the veterans affairs committee in 1948 who would have agreed that this woman's earnings from going out doing that odd housework should be considered as anything other than casual earnings. I therefore suggest to the minister that he have his war veterans' allowance board up on the carpet and inquire from them exactly how they decide what earnings are casual.
Then there are rulings of another type which I think are unfair. They have to do with the question of whether or not a person under the ordinary eligible age is incapable of maintaining himself. The pertinent section of the act is section 5, paragraph (c) (ii) which reads as follows:
is incapable and unlikely to become capable of maintaining himself or herself because of economic handicaps-[DOT]
And I point out to the minister that phrase "because of economic handicaps".
*-combined with mental or physical disability or insufficiency.
This particular case was that of a widow who herself had service. She herself was eligible if she could satisfy the requirements of the act. She is fifty years of age, whereas the eligible age for a woman who has served is fifty-five. Her husband served in both wars. She has a son about thirteen years of age who is asthmatic, a semi-invalid. The woman herself is not well; she has arthritis and other disabilities. Her application for war veterans' allowance was turned down on the ground that she was capable of maintaining herself. Can you, Mr. Speaker, imagine a widow in that position being told that she must go out and get a job? "Actually she went to the employment service where she was told: "Why, you are fifty years of age! What are you coming around here for, looking for a job? We cannot find you any work." Yet just two or three weeks ago that woman was again held by the board to be ineligible. I had arranged for her to go and have an examination by her doctor. I turned in that examination in Vancouver, but for some reason or other it has not reached the office here, and the board did not get it sent back before they made their decision. This case brings up another point on which 1 suggest that the minister check his board.
Another matter is this question of overpayments. It is found that a man has beer getting more earnings than he is entitled tc

while getting his allowance. Far too often, word of those overpayments does not get back to the veteran until months have gone by and then he finds himself suddenly faced with a large debit to be taken off his meagre monthly allowance. In some cases a man will have his pension raised, and instead of that adjustment being made in the minister's department at that time when the pension is raised, the war veterans' allowance board apparently does not find out about the raise for months. The man gets the increased pension, and then suddenly he is faced with a notice that he has been overpaid several hundred dollars war veterans' allowance. That is a matter of poor administration and it should be checked. When these pensions are raised, the adjustment should be made at the same time. There is no excuse for a thing like that happening in the one department.
Another difficulty is this question of deductions while the man is in hospital. He goes into hospital, and a deduction is made from his allowance. I think the figure is usually $15 a month. I suggest that this whole policy of deducting money from the war veterans' allowance while the recipient is in hospital should be carefully reviewed. In many cases I think there is a great unfairness. Mind you, I have drawn several of these cases to the attention of the board, and in most instances some reduction has been made in the amount taken from the veteran. The allowances are so small, Mr. Speaker, that when you take $5 or $10 or $15 off, it creates a serious problem for the wife and the children. I think we might well stop making these deductions at all.
One other suggestion is that the treatment rates should be reconsidered. In some cases apparently the war veterans' allowance recipients are not getting the same treatment rates that they formerly received. There, I believe, is another field for an investigation by the department. Those are some of the things which I think show that the administration of the War Veterans Allowance Act is not what it should be, and I hope that the minister will check the administration.
In conclusion, may I say that I sincerely believe it has been a great mistake not to have a special committee of the house on veterans affairs at this session; in fact, I believe there should be a standing committee on veterans affairs. These problems could all be dealt with efficiently by such a committee of the house. That is the proper way to settle them. The Legion, the Army and Navy Veterans, the Amps., the Canadian Corps and the Canadian Pension Association and all these veterans' organizations which
War Veterans Allowance Act have been so responsible in their approach to the veterans' problems could appear before such a committee and explain their experiences to the members. In my experience they have always done that in an efficient and fair way. We have all benefited as a result of their representations. The officers of the department could be brought before the committee and could give their explanations. With regard to some of the instances I have mentioned tonight perhaps those officers could explain why the trouble has arisen. But that clearing of ideas and that facing of problems can only be adequately done by a committee of this house.
When I asked the parliamentary assistant about a committee on December 10 last year he gave this answer, which may be found at page 3137 of Hansard:
On the other hand, if he means that,-
He was referring to myself because I had suggested a special- committee in the 1950 session.
On the other hand, if he means that, when changes are being made in veterans legislation, the government will continue the practice it has been following since 1936, namely, referring the bill to a select committee of the House of Commons, I should hope that practice would be continued.
The parliamentary assistant has been a member of every veterans affairs committee since 1935, just as I have myself. There was his statement, that whenever veterans legislation was before the house it should be referred to a special committee. Certainly, amending the War Veterans Allowance Act comes within that category, especially when you are changing the administration. This bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act is of the utmost importance. I repeat, it should be referred to a select committee of the house. I hope that even at this late date the government will agree that such a course could very well be followed.

Certainly I have not acquired any wisdom from following the speeches of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Whatever wisdom there may be, I am able to stand on my own two feet and express myself without any help from anybody.
This is a matter of very great concern to hon. members, and it is perhaps of more concern to British Columbia members than to any others, because I think we are much closer to the problem for two or three reasons. First of all, we are very proud that in the last war we had the highest per capita enlistment of any province of Canada so we have more B.C. veterans returning home. Second, our province is especially attractive, except for the last winter, to older veterans, because of what is generally a more equable climate than is experienced in most of Canada. We therefore have a steady


trek of old veterans out to British Columbia. Third, we have a higher concentration of old imperial veterans, because our province has always had a very heavy settlement by immigrants from the British isles. For that reason British Columbia members, whether they be Liberals, Conservatives, or members of the C.C.F., have always been more conscious of the problems of the older veterans.
We have another reason for being exercised. In British Columbia the old age pension, as has been frequently mentioned in this house, is the highest in Canada. The basic $40 a month pension, three-quarters of which is paid by the federal government and one-quarter by the provincial government, is augmented in British Columbia by another $10 with no extra means test. That means in effect that the old age pension in British Columbia is $50 a month.
The intent of the war veterans' allowance has always been, to my mind, a pension paid ten years earlier to those who have been prematurely aged because .they saw service in a combat area. And that immediately brings up this one standard. Should the federal government not be able to match the very best old age pension age by any province, and that is our present standard in British Columbia? No matter what is said, we feel very strongly that the pension paid by the federal government-as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) said, to those pensioners who are an especial responsibility of the federal government, that is the war veterans just as locally the old age pensioner is the especial responsibility of the provincial government-should at least match the most generous old age pension in Canada.
I just want to give an example which was given to me in a village in my own riding, the little village where my mother and father are now retired. Near that village there are a German immigrant couple who actually were in Germany during the first war. No doubt they are very decent people. They came out after the war and now have their twenty years' residence in Canada. They did not attempt to join any company pension scheme, and they may not have been able to make any savings in war bonds, so now that they have reached the age of 70 they get $100 a month from the government as an old age pension. As far as most people are concerned, they are not very interested in the levels of government, whether it is municipal government, provincial government or federal government; they are getting it from the government. This German couple-unfortunately they are still referred to as a German couple-were in Germany during the first war, and they now get $100 a month, and they

live very comfortably on the west coast of British Columbia in a little village on $100 a month. Contrast them with a couple living not very many cottages away. In that cottage is a man who served very bravely in the first war, and who now is prematurely aged, the very thing that this legislation passed by this government was meant to cover. He and his wife live out there on $70 a month. That is the basic federal war veterans allowance, commonly called the burnt out pension. True, by going through an extra means test, which the hon. member for Fraser Valley described, they might be able to get another $10. No matter how well this has worked in the east, it has not worked in British Columbia and the basic allowance remains $70. So, as British Columbians, from whatever party we may come, but especially as British Columbia veterans, we say that the federal government should be able to match for their "wards", which is perhaps an unfortunate word to use, but the comparison is accurate-for their special old age pensioners-as good treatment, as high a pension, as that paid by any of the provinces. That is the first point I wish to make. I think I have expressed the view of every hon. member from British Columbia, because we live with the problem.
My second point has to do with the imperial veterans. I recall that in the 1946 committee-I have been reminded of it many times by Legion branches-I voted against the extension of war veterans' allowances to imperial veterans. There was, however, a vote preceding that vote to extend the war veterans' allowances to Canadians of the first war who had got to England but not to France. In the last war if a veteran got to England he was qualified, as far as service was concerned, for the war veterans' allowance but in the first world war he had to get past England to France. I have always in this house tried to argue that in every service there should be a uniformity of service, whether it is the air force, the army or the navy, a thing which has now been brought about by the legislation sponsored by the Minister of National Defence. I say also that between the first and second wars there should be a uniformity of service. If service in England qualifies a man in the second war for a burnt-out pension, then I maintain that service in England in the first war should also qualify a Canadian veteran for a burnt-out pension. I voted for this in the veterans affairs committee and when that was denied to Canadians who are the proper responsibility of the Canadian government, then I felt I could not vote to give this Canadian pension to men who did not serve
20, 1950
War Veterans Allowance Act in the Canadian forces, and who were not resident in Canada before their entry into the British forces.
We have been very generous in Canada, more generous than any other country I know of, when we build up to Canadian standards the pensions of men who may have lived in this country before the war, but who saw service in other allied armies. When they have come back here we have regarded them as Canadians and built up their pensions to the Canadian standard. The government has now come along and done something further. Perhaps there war a strong moral obligation to these imperials, who came out here after the first war and became good Canadians, to say to them, "All right, we will include you in our war veterans' allowance scheme", as we are doing tonight but there has never been any legal obligation.
I think too, with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), that, having included them, we should do it right. It is unfair to cut out this one little group, the widows of imperial veterans who may have died. I say that the widow of any imperial veteran who qualified by having resided twenty years in this country should qualify, just as does the widow of a Canadian recipient of the war veterans' allowance.
That is my only complaint about this very generous extension of the war veterans' allowance into a field in which we have no legal responsibility; because these imperial veterans we are covering now did not live in Canada before they fought, and they did not fight with Canadian forces. They came here after the war.
I saw a very interesting sidelight in connection with that in my recent trip to Europe -which was described this afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) in most unflattering terms-because I had representations made to me on behalf of one of the British branches of the Canadian Legion. They complained bitterly about this proposed extension of the war veterans' allowance to imperial veterans when they, as Canadian veterans in Great Britain, received no such allowances from the British government.
So I say we are taking a very real forward step in veterans legislation. There is one further thing I wish to say however-because I still feel some responsibility in the matter of taxation. Those people who are advocating these extensions should not be too critical about the taxing system which, after all, must find the money to pay for all this. I would like to see some members who are asking for this increased benefit speak in less

These extensions to imperial veterans are increased payments which, while desirable, must be paid for.
I pay tribute to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) because I have the pleasure now and again-not much of a pleasure- to sit in on treasury board which apportions federal revenue to the government departments. No one on treasury board works any harder to get his share of the national revenue for the benefit of the veterans than does the present Minister of Veterans Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few moments to deal with this most important resolution. I do feel however that I should lend support to the previous speakers who have supported it, and who have expressed their disappointment that other amendments are not included in the proposed legislation.
Before proceeding to my remarks on the resolution let me pay tribute to what I believe has been a most effective and efficient operation of the war veterans' allowance board. I have had some experience in dealing with it, through the local representatives 'in British Columbia, and I must say in all fairness that I have found them most courteous and most anxious in every way possible to use the legislation at their hands and the administrative machinery to the best advantage of the veterans concerned.
I am sure all hon. members are pleased to note that the minister has seen fit to introduce this resolution which will precede the legislation to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act so as to include within the terms of the act imperial veterans who have lived in Canada twenty years or more. Not only will hon. members be pleased, but I am sure the 3,000-odd members of the imperial veterans mentioned by the minister will be gratified indeed.
As I stand here this evening I can think of a good many cases in my own riding concerning men who will be greatly benefited by this legislation. The Canadian Legion and other veterans organization across Canada will be deeply gratified that their long-time advocacy of this legislation and this amendment has reached fruition.
In common with other members who have spoken, I regret the government has not seen fit to include the widows of imperial veterans who at this time will have resided in Canada for twenty years. It is most unfortunate, because I do not think the numbers


are large and the expense to the country would not be great. When the minister tells us that this amendment will cost about $2 million, it seems he has been somewhat parsimonious in failing to include in the legislation widows of imperial veterans who have resided in Canada for twenty years.
I believe the minister said that the total cost of war veterans' allowances to the taxpayers of Canada would be approximately $25 million, including the cost occasioned by this amendment. If we look at this question objectively and fairly in relation to our national income and our total revenue, that $25 million is not a large amount to spend in providing at least a measure of security for those who have served the country so well.
In connection with the suggestion that the legislation should include the widows of imperial veterans who have resided in this country twenty years, I am sure any action taken by the minister to include such an amendment to the bill would receive the widespread support of the Canadian people. I have received resolutions from branches of the Canadian Legion, other organizations and a large number of individuals, and I would say that no one can point to a single occasion when legislation introduced in the House of Commons to improve the position of veterans in this country has not received almost unanimous endorsation from the Canadian people. I do hope therefore that consideration will be given to the suggestion made by previous speakers so as to include in the amendment the relatively small number of widows of imperial veterans thus far forgotten.
Before resuming my seat may I say a word about the special assistance fund. I have no hesitation in saying that in my experience the special assistance fund has been beneficial to many veterans. I have seen this in my own district, so far as individuals are concerned, and I am familiar with the benefit which has resulted. But, in common with many other members, I believe that this is insufficient. While it is a great help, the only fair solution is to accept the proposals of the Canadian Legion and to increase the basic rate to $50 for single men and $85 for married men. That is little enough when compared with the pension to the old age pensioner paid in some provinces of Canada, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), and the hon. member for Fraser Valley

(Mr. Cruickshank), who is always a most effective exponent of veterans legislation, and other hon. members.
Previous speakers have dealt with the increased old age pensions paid by certain provinces which are greater than war veterans' allowances. I thought they dealt most effectively with that matter. I was taken with the illustration given by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) of the former German citizen who was residing in Germany at the time of the first world war, who came to this country, and now is receiving, along with his wife, an old age pension totalling $100 a month, whereas the war veteran who was defending his country at that time receives only slightly over $70 per month. We do not question the old age pension paid to the other persons, for no doubt they are good citizens; but I personally cannot see any justice in a situation like that. The allowances paid to our veterans should at least be equal to those received by old age pensioners.
In British Columbia old age pensioners are covered by the health insurance scheme but are not required to pay, whereas recipients of war veterans' allowances are. Just before I left home a few days ago to return to Ottawa I met a war veteran who is in receipt of an allowance. He served in my battalion and the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra knows him quite well. This man's wife has been quite ill and he himself suffers from partial blindness and is thus unable to earn a living. He is an aged man and is now in receipt of war veterans' allowance. He applied for the special allowance of $10 per month, but still finds great difficulty in getting along.
He was confronted with a bill from the hospital insurance commission of British Columbia. He went to the office of the commission and told the officials that he was completely unable to pay the bill. I might mention that he was decorated in the first world war and served with the 54th battalion, one of the finest battalions in the Canadian expeditionary force. Later he received a note that if he did not pay immediately he would be prosecuted. He went to see the official of the hospital commission and told her that he could not pay, that if they desired to prosecute he was ready to go to jail. The official then said to him. "As a matter of fact, our instructions are to get it out of you if we can, but if we realize that it is not possible for you to pay we are not to take any action." Imagine a man who has served our country so well being placed in that position. An amendment to
War Veterans Allowance Act the act would relieve the condition of that man and other veterans to a considerable extent.
The minister mentioned changes to be made in the act to provide for decentralization in administration. That will be all to the good. I am in favour of decentralization in connection with government or other public business because the closer you get your administration to the people, the more sympathetic and efficient it is likely to be. I am sure the amendments proposed by the minister in this connection will further improve the administration of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Before resuming my seat I want to indicate my support of other hon. members who have urged the establishment of a parliamentary committee on veterans affairs. That is necessary if we are going to tackle these problems effectively and efficiently, to the advantage of the veteran and the satisfaction of the Canadian people as a whole. I urge the minister and his colleagues to give further consideration to the requests that have been made from all sides-I was glad to hear hon. members on the other side speak in this connection-for the establishment of a special parliamentary committee on veterans affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall attempt to follow the example of the last two speakers and confine my remarks within a brief compass. At the outset I want to associate myself, as they have done, with the remarks that have been made in appreciation of the fact that the minister has seen fit to introduce these amendments enlarging the scope of the act to include imperial veterans. This is being done no doubt as a result of the study he has given the matter, and also I am sure partly because of the extraordinarily reasonable and competent representations that have been made from time to time by the Canadian Legion and other veterans' bodies.
Having said this, I want also to associate myself with those who, while giving due credit for this move, have requested that advantage be taken of this opportunity to complete the good work which will be carried out in the legislation based on this resolution, and not stop short of what humanity, reason and justice dictate; particularly not to stop short of extending these benefits to the widows of imperial veterans. After all, Mr. Speaker, those widows are already so much worse off as a result of their widowhood. I am not seeking here to assess the humanitarian aspects, which goes without saying; but the tragedy and bereavement they have suffered only emphasize the material aspect of it. These widows are worse off and less able to get along in the world because they have lost their husbands. In spite of that disadvantage, however, in this legislation we are only extending benefits to veterans and their wives who in a material sense are so much better off than the widow who has lost her husband. To that extent we are increasing a disparity which already exists if

we extend these benefits to the veterans and their wives and deny them to the widows merely because their husbands died before they had resided in this country for twenty years.
I know the minister is just as open to humanitarian appeals as anyone in the house. I hope he will see the force of that argument and allow himself to be moved by that situation, if I may put it that way, and give the matter further consideration. I know he must have considered it already; I know it has been brought to his attention. In a sense we are not advancing new arguments, but we are asking him to open his mind to the arguments already put forward. I would ask him to bear in mind that if we are unsuccessful in prevailing upon him to enlarge the scope of this legislation, then we are in fact increasing a disparity which already exists and prolonging as well as accentuating a hardship which it would cost so little to remove.
Then, dealing with two or three other details, I want to associate myself with those who have referred to the amount of the basic war veterans' allowance. I know the attitude of the parliamentary assistant in this matter, at any rate, and I presume he speaks for the government and for his minister. His attitude, which is a perfectly proper one for him to take, is that in essence the war veterans' allowance is merely an old age pension payable to war veterans at an earlier date by reason of the fact that, by virtue of their service and the hardships they suffered, they become unable to provide for themselves at an earlier age than the ordinary citizen. Taking that view the hon. gentleman has stated that he would not consider it proper that the amount of the war veterans' allowance should be larger than the basic old age pension or, in other words, more than $40 a month.
While I agree that this is a reasonable attitude for him to take, I cannot agree that his basic premise is correct. I do not believe the war veterans' allowance is merely an old age pension payable at an earlier age. It seems to me, and from my recollection of veterans' affairs committees it has been recognized, that there are two aspects combined. One is the reward for service over and above what the ordinary civilian or non-service man has given. The other is a certain recognition of the fact that by virtue of the service given and the hardship experienced he may become unable to provide for himself at an earlier age than the civilian.
If this war veterans' allowance has a dual aspect, then surely it is not sound to argue that the amount should be exactly the same as the basic old age pension. Even if that

In the province of British Columbia that is $50 per month, and in several other provinces it is $40 per month, by virtue of special supplementary payments made by the provinces.
Whichever way you look at it, it seems to me there is a sound, logical, unanswerable case for increasing the amount of the war veterans' allowance to $50 for single men and $85 for married veterans. Those are the two main aspects of this matter to which I should like to address myself tonight. I wonder if I could mention one detail of the administration.
I fully agree that it is time to decentralize the administration of this act. I have had cases where, apparently with the best will in the world to speed up the investigation and disposition of the case, it has still taken months, in fact nearly a year, to complete a case from the preliminary application to the final disposition. It seems to me that no administration should take from six to nine months to settle a case finally. I cannot help concluding that if there were greater decentralization, if a greater measure of responsibility were given not only to the regional offices but to the investigators themselves, who should be given greater discretion in arriving at a decision as to whether or not the means test, if it is to be continued, should be applied, whether or not in fact the veteran has casual earnings or whether the earnings he receives should form part of his basic income, and if the investigators were given greater discretion to recommend for or against granting the allowance to the veteran, then that, coupled with the decentralization of responsibility, would greatly speed up the disposition of cases.
It seems to me that at the present time the regulations are so ironclad, and the feeling seems to be that we must follow precedent to such an extent that, even with the greatest desire to bring a. veteran within the scope of the act, investigators have to go back and back again before they can satisfy their superiors that the veteran is entitled to the allowance. I hope that along with the decentralization of administration will come a greater measure of responsibility, and the power of recommendation to the investigators in the field. If that does accompany decentralization, and if there is an increase in the

Mr. Speaker,
I did not intend to speak on this subject, so I shall only take three or four minutes of the time of the house. 'There are a few things I wish to suggest. First of all, I should like to congratulate the minister on this resolution, which I think is a definite step forward. It shows careful thought and sincerity of purpose.
A number of suggestions have been made by various hon. members, and generally speaking I believe the suggestions have been worth while. They have concerned the type of thing we would all like to see implemented. I have heard very few things mentioned in connection with this resolution which I, personally, would not like to see implemented. I do wish to put forward the definite suggestion to hon. members of this house that this is not a question of spending unlimited funds, and giving all the things we would like to see on the statute books of this country. It is a question of having a certain amount of money to spend, and spending it in the wisest possible way.
The member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has suggested that the amount of the basic war veterans' allowance should be increased. The same suggestion has been made by other hon. members, and I can find no fault with that; it would be a forward step. But let us face facts. We have so much money to spend, and while these suggestions are worthy, and I think they will be implemented some day when the income of this country is sufficient to pay for them, we simply cannot afford everything we would like. In a sense it is rather a waste of time to place all these schemes before the house, and ask that the minister give them his earnest consideration. The minister is giving these matters his earnest consideration. The minister is not only a gallant soldier but a gallant gentleman, and no one would like to do these things more than he, but he cannot give something he has not got. Putting all these schemes before the house is not only premature, but to be frank I think it is silly.
I wish to try to give the members some understanding of the problems of the government. There is a tendency in all the parties in the house, and I do not blame them, because it is a tendency of human nature, to ask for things which they genuinely feel


everyone should have. Many of these things I should like to see done, but it does seem to be consuming a great deal of time when these speakers, who are intelligent, must realize that there are not the funds available at this time to implement such schemes. I suggest that an enormous amount of time is wasted by certain hon. members, who are sincere, owing to the fact that they feel certain things should be done, even though they realize there are no funds with which to do them. I would suggest to those members, who doubtless mean well, that they should leave these things in the hands of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), who is highly qualified and who receives expert advice from various sections of his department. I want to thank the minister for interrupting and making that point clear. I had hoped and had dared to believe that that was the situation. The next comment I should like to make is in relation to the continuing plea for the War Veterans Allowance Act to be amended so as to include the veterans of world war I who got only as far as England. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) has already stated the case quite well so that I need not go into it further, but there is just this that I want to say. On March 16 of this year, as recorded at page 841 of Hansard, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs answered two questions of mine which were as follows:
1.	How many Canadian veterans of world war I, not now eligible for any benefits under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act, could qualify for an allowance thereunder if the United Kingdom were declared a theatre of war in world war I for the purposes of the said act?
2.	How many widows of Canadian veterans 'of world war I, not now eligible for any benefits under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act, could qualify for an allowance thereunder if the United Kingdom were declared a theatre of war in world war I for the purposes of the said act?
War Veterans Allowance Act
This is the answer:

Statistics covering these categories
have never been compiled.
Estimated number of veterans alive today who served during world war I in the United Kingdom but not in an actual theatre of war as presently defined in the War Veterans Allowance Act: 51,000.
Then there is another sentence that I need not bother to give, and another paragraph in that answer says that the estimated number of widows of veterans who got only to England in world war I would be 7,600.
Some who have looked at these figures have said to me that the large number of them seems to be the reason for the government not acceding to our request that they be included under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act. I understand, however, that as to the 33,000 veterans who are on the war veterans allowance, they represent something in the neighbourhood of 15 per cent of the total number of veterans alive today who saw service in world war I in an actual theatre of war and qualify for war veterans allowance if they meet the means test and other provisions. I think it would be fair to assume that the percentage of those who got only to England and the percentage of widows of those who got only to England would be no higher than the percentage of those who got into France. As a matter of fact, I would imagine that the percentage might be a little bit lower.
All I wanted to do in this portion of my remarks was to point out that if you reduce those figures to 15 per cent, it leaves you with about 7,000 veterans-or a little over- who got only to England in world war I who might qualify if England were made a theatre of war for that war. Similarly, the number of widows of veterans of world war I, where the veteran got to England but did not get to France, would probably not be over 1,000. I realize that those figures, 7,000 veterans and 1,000 widows, are more in number than the number being brought in under the provision that is before us in this resolution; but they still are not extensive numbers and they are a good deal less than the estimates that the parliamentary assistant placed on Hansard at page 841.	-
Despite what the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) has just said, I feel that we are not asking for too much in pressing our point that England should be made a theatre of war in world war I as it is in world war II and that there should be that uniformity of treatment of veterans and their widows. I hope the point will be considered further, and favourably.
I also want to support those who have argued that the time has come for the amount of the allowance to be increased. Excellent

War \ cterans Allowance Act arguments have been made tonight on all sides for this increase; and as the minister probably knows, he will have equally excellent arguments placed before him in a week or so when representatives of the non-pen-sioned veterans' widows come to Ottawa again and seek an audience with him. I was disappointed earlier in the session when he indicated that he was not at that time prepared to recommend to cabinet that the request of that association be given consideration. I hope that in the weeks that have gone by since then further consideration may have been given to the matter and that we may get at least the figures that have been mentioned tonight, the figures proposed by the Legion, the figures that were mentioned in the resolution by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode), of $50 a month for a single veteran, $85 a month for a married veteran, and $50 a month in the case of a widow.
The next comment I should like to make is in relation to something else that was said earlier this evening. I think it is sometimes referred to as the case of a veteran under domiciliary care. It seems unfair that the wife of a veteran in hospital should suffer the reduction in her income that is the case under the regulations as they now stand. It has been suggested to me-and I think it is a reasonable request-that the wife of a veteran on burnt out pension, who has to go to hospital, should get not less than she will get if she becomes a widow. That happens at the present time. The wife of the veteran who has had to go to hospital, a veteran on burnt out pension, may be cut down pretty low in the amount that she will get; but if the veteran dies and she meets the various qualifications, she may get the $40.41 a month that is now being paid, or $50 a month which we hope will soon be the case. I simply put that suggestion before the minister, that in that situation the amount paid to the wife of a veteran in hospital should certainly not be less than the amount of the allowance that is available to a widow under this act.
One other thought, Mr. Speaker, and I shall take my seat. A good deal has been said this evening by way of comparing the burnt out pension with the old age pension. The comments that have been made were very much to the point, and hon. members generally have appreciated their force. I should like to say this. It seems to me that it would simplify the whole business, and would be a lot fairer to all concerned, if we could soon get to the point where old age pension was paid to all without a means test. I am doing my best toward that end. Then the people who are now made recipients of war veterans
[Mr. Knowles.!

allowances could be made recipients of that proper old age pension at an earlier age. After all, that is what the war veterans allowance was thought to be in the first instance; but as it stands it imposes what is sometimes referred to as a social service burden on the Department of Veterans Affairs. The result is you have two separate means test programs now in effect, namely, the one with respect to the old age pension, and the one with respect to the burnt out pension. It seems to me the simplest way to do it would be for the government-this is a problem not only for the Minister of Veterans Affairs; it is a problem for the government as a whole-to get as quickly as possible to a proper old age pension without a means test. Veterans then who are at whatever age has been decided upon for the old age pension would get it in full without any question, and the legislation could include a provision that veterans ten years younger than the age for the old age pension be entitled to draw that pension at that earlier age, because of their service and because of what that service has done by causing them to age earlier. It might be a good idea for the Minister of Veterans Affairs, or his parliamentary assistant, to draw up a brief and come before our committee on old age security and urge that that be done.
Again I am glad to see the Minister of Veterans Affairs nodding his head. And if a motion is necessary to hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs, or his parliamentary assistant, I am sure that the hon. member to my right, the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), will be glad to join with me in seeing that that motion is put before the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the resolution as proposed by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg). I am in full agreement with the amendment as brought before the house to extend assistance to veterans other than Canadian citizens at the time of enlistment, and especially with the provision which the minister has incorporated in the resolution, namely, to include former members of the forces of His Majesty's allies who have resided in Canada for not less than twenty years. I think that is a very fair provision.
I am thinking, Mr. Speaker, of another group of war service veterans who were Canadian citizens when they enlisted in the Canadian forces. I have had many letters appealing to me to make recommendations on their behalf. They have written to various Legion branches in some instances. I am referring now particularly to returned veterans of Prince Edward Island who fought with the Canadian forces in the two last wars. Many of these veterans have appealed to me on the ground that their appeals and requests for assistance under the War Veterans Allowance Act and the war veterans pension act have been rejected. They feel very keenly that they have not been used fairly. They feel that they have not been used as they should have been used. They also feel, as do many of their fellow citizens who are non-veterans, like myself, that those men should be accorded better treatment by the department than they have received in the past. I am not criticizing the government nor the Minister of Veterans Affairs in this connection; but I believe that many of these marginal cases that are examined by medical doctors should receive the benefit of the doubt. I do not wish to cause any alarm over the situation, but I do wish to say, as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) said, that the Canadian veteran has been treated as well as, and possibly better than, any other veteran in the world with the possible exception of the veterans who fought with the United States forces.
Yesterday I had a request from a veteran of the first world war. His case is conspicuous. He enlisted and was placed in category A. He was sent to England, and in preparation for training along the English channel he contracted rheumatism. He was sent before the medical officer, placed in category C and returned to Canada. On making application
20. 1950
War Veterans Allowance Act for some assistance under the War Veterans Allowance Act he was told that the expiry date for receiving such applications was in the year 1936. I am not sure of the date, but it is immaterial. This case appeals to me and I have had one or two other cases brought to my attention. One of these, for instance, was where a war veteran had died and the widow did not receive the pension after the veteran's death. I cannot see any condition that should result in such a decision by the board where, after a veteran has died leaving a widow and a small family, the pension should be discontinued.
In closing my remarks may I repeat that I am fully in accord with the resolution extending the benefits to veterans other than those who were Canadian citizens when they enlisted. But I am appealing to the minister and the government to try to satisfy those needy cases concerning veterans who were Canadian citizens when they enlisted. It would be a grave mistake in connection with the administration of the various acts of government concerned with veterans affairs if a shadow were cast over this beneficial legislation because it did not include those cases where veterans have not received what they considered justice, or received what was not considered justice by ordinary citizens.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that at long last a measure of this kind has been introduced. Since I came to the House of Commons in 1945 veterans' organizations in Canada have been pressing for the inclusion of the so-called imperial veterans under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act. It certainly marks a distinct step forward to have these benefits under the act thus extended.
I am sorry to see that when this is being done the benefits are not at the same time being extended to those Canadian soldiers who served only in England during the first world war. That matter has been discussed at some length already, so I shall not do more than mention it. I am also disappointed that the amount of the war veterans' allowance is not being increased to at least the amount of old age pensions.
I am glad to hear that some members on the government side of the house are in support of the idea that the allowance should be increased, and also that Canadians who served only in England should be included in the act.
I believe it was the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Hunter) who spoke at some length about the expense of doing this, and made the suggestion that it should not be expected that these benefits should be extended to a

War Veterans Allowance Act point where expenses would be unduly increased. May I point out to him and to any others who may have similar ideas that it is only as a result of at least five years of constant effort that the present provision has been introduced so as to extend the benefits of the act to the imperial veterans. It is only by talking constantly about these matters and urging their necessity that we make progress.
So far as the expense involved is concerned, I think it has been indicated by some hon. members already that the expense would not be great. Let me add only this, that the amount of money it would cost could be readily saved by the government's cutting out some of its expensive agencies, and the large amounts spent in travelling expenses and the like. Perhaps these decreases would have good results, even in the departments concerned, and certainly it would be beneficial for the veterans.
Let me speak briefly about the so-called increase granted a year or so ago. The general impression that went out to the country was that war veterans' allowances were being increased by $10 a month. That was not the case. As a matter of fact this $10 was a welfare allowance contingent upon a means test. So far as I know, no one in that part of the country from which I come has received the benefit of that $10; no matter how desperate his circumstances may have been, he just did not get it. How desperate people had to be to get that $10, I do not know; but I do know that three or four people who came to me, and whose cases I took up with the department, were not able to get it. How one's circumstances could be much worse than the circumstances in those cases, it is difficult to imagine.
I do not wish to discuss these matters to any great extent, but I do think a point made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has some bearing in this connection, and that is that the payment of these war veterans' allowances to people who qualify under the new provisions should be made retroactive to the date on which it was first announced it should be paid. Announcements of this kind raise hopes in people's minds when they know they qualify and will subsequently come under the act. It is a bitter thing, a disappointing thing, to have the allowance promised and then to have it delayed, delayed, delayed, indefinitely. Eventually when it does come, having expected it for so long, this hope deferred has a rather bad effect. From that point of view particularly I suggest payment should be made retroactive at least to the first of this year.
I believe the decentralization feature is a good one. One of the difficulties I have

encountered in various cases which have come to my attention has been the high degree of complaint concerning the red tape involved and the length of time it takes to have the matter cleared up. In some cases an allowance is cut down. The length of time it takes to find out why it has been cut, and to have the matter reviewed, and in some cases adjusted, or some satisfactory explanation given, is in many cases quite out of proportion. Decentralization of authority in the hands of local boards who can handle these matters will get away from much of that difficulty, and make the working of the act more humane and more satisfactory to the recipients.
The desirability of having a standing committee on veterans affairs has been urged by several other hon. members, and I shall only mention it at this time. I believe a considerable number of complaints by veterans could be handled readily and with great advantage to the government and the veterans themselves through the establishment of a committee of that kind. Again I would strongly urge upon the government that such a committee be established.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
