speechtext: May we have some further clarification regarding the allowance which would be paid to the widows of imperial pensioners? If an imperial pensioner dies before his 20 years' residence in this country has expired, but his widow has continued to live on here and has resided in Canada for twenty years, will she or will she not be in receipt of the allowance?

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: No; if the veteran died prior to spending twenty years in Canada, then his widow would not be eligible. As I interjected before, there had to be a time somewhere as a base from which to start. That was twenty years' residence in Canada. One can go back and visualize a veteran coming from Scotland in 1920 with his wife and dying the day he arrived in Halifax. That would be an extreme case. Where between that and the 20-year period would you draw the line? In order to bring these veterans into the same position as those now receiving war veterans' allowances the 20-year residence was taken as the basic factor. If a man came to this country in 1920, lived here until 1940 and died, his wife would be eligible to apply.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: But the veteran himself must live in Canada for the 20 years?

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: I was urging that the widow of a veteran who had herself lived in Canada for 20 years should receive the benefits of the act.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: If she had service in her own right.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: Then she would be a veteran herself. The representations that have been made to me have been made on behalf of widows of veterans who died before the 20-year period was up. Has the minister made any inquiry as to how many such widows there are in Canada, that is, widows of imperial veterans who lived here for a certain period of time and then passed away before 20 years' residence had been completed?

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: In connection with this whole matter of war veterans' allowances and pensions, the widow as such has no rights except those from her veteran husband. In the case of old age pensions the widow would be a person in her own right. If she had never had a husband she could receive an old age pension when she reached a certain age. In this case the allowance is provided to the veteran for the wife while he is alive so that he may have more for himself, if you want to take a selfish view. We studied this matter carefully and could not see the equity of treating the widows of this group any different from those who are already in receipt of war veterans' allowances. If we made it possible for widows of veterans of this group who were in the country for only a year or two to qualify, when we were taking the 20-year period in Canada as essential for the veteran himself before he could qualify, we felt that there would be inequity. Twenty years has been taken as the basic period, both for the veteran himself and for his widow.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: It is not 20 years for the widow; it is 20 years for the veteran. It does not matter how long the widow may have lived here. After all, the widow has been in partnership with the veteran. The widow of a Canadian veteran who was eligible for war veterans' allowances is entitled to an allowance when she reaches 55 years of age.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
Surely the same principle should apply in this case. There does not seem to be any equity about it. Here is a woman who has lived in Canada for 20 years. If her husband had lived in Canada for 20 years she would be entitled to war veterans' allowance. Because he died, is her postiion any better? If her husband dies is her position so much better? Surely she should receive consideration if she has lived in this country for 20 years. She would have received consideration if her husband had continued to
War Veterans Allowance Act live, but if he has died her position will be more pitiful and she is deprived of the opportunity to receive the allowance that she would have got had her husband lived. We hear about equity but I do not think there is any equity about it.

Before the minister answers I should like to ask him a question. We have heard a lot about the widows of imperial veterans, and Canada is generous to them.
I should like to know how many veterans of the Canadian armed services are receiving pensions in Great Britain from the British government. To my knowledge the number would be small, but I would be most interested to have some information about it.
While I am addressing you, sir, I should like to make two other observations. The first has to do with the two secretaries of the minister, Colonel Macbeth and Mr. Bosse. They are most helpful to hon. members who get in touch with them, and I take this opportunity to pay my tribute to them. I can tell you, however, that we have many difficulties with the pension commission. If the returned men were fairly dealt with by that commission there would be no need for allowances.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: Order.

speechtext:
I will explain the link between the first and second parts of my argument.
I am perfectly in order in making that comparison between pensions and allowances because a pension is a matter of right, a debt of the state to a man who has served in one of the three branches of the armed forces. On the other hand an allowance is temporary, a sort of gift or donation. If we have allowances to returned men it is precisely because the pension commission has done nothing for them, or has not done enough. Sometimes a little bonus is given by the allowance branch of the department to men already in receipt of pensions because those pensions are too small. This is nonsense. Such cases should be reviewed by the commission and such men should be dealt with as they deserve, as a matter of right. I have had this in mind to say for a long time.
It is surprising how many reasons the pension commission can find for refusing an application on behalf of a returned man. Not only that; in many cases men suffer from disabilities resulting from their service, and undoubtedly are entitled to pension. That is the spirit and letter of the act. Nothing is given them, however, because the pension commission is inactive and serves very little purpose except to refuse applications. Then we have to call upon the allowance board to


redress the wrongs caused by the pension commission. That is pretty hard to think of. The minister has been most fair with me, but he knows I want to have as little as possible to do with the pension commission. I am fed up with them; it is a waste of time.
As to the allowance board, they are supposedly economical, and give allowances with a dropper. It is not an open tap, just a dropper in most cases. I give the minister credit; he has one of the finest war records, and he does his best when any case is submitted to him. But we strike an obstacle at once, and that obstacle is always the pension commission. The men who make up that commission have fine war records, but that is no defence when we have a justifiable claim that is rejected. I know of many men who cannot get justice from this pension board, and I complain bitterly about it as a member of parliament and as a friend of the soldiers. How is it that some cases dating back to the first war have not been settled yet? 1 know some men who were powerfully built. They were in the trenches for many months, sleeping in the mud, suffering from cold-

speechtext: While these men apparently were in class A at the time of their discharge, later they were found to be suffering from disabilities due to war service that had not appeared at that time. That is why they were not dealt with at a time when the pension commission was more generous than it is now.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER

speechtext:
May I suggest to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that he give consideration to making the test the date the veteran came to Canada. If he came to Canada twenty years ago, the widow should be eligible. I think that is the idea we all had, but on the basis of the minister's statement no widow whose husband died before 1940 can possibly establish eligibility. None of these imperials came here before 1920. Many of them came after that, up to as late as 1930. If the act is to read as the minister suggests, the widow of a man who came here in 1930 and is now dead has no possible chance of getting the allowance. I do not think the proposal made by the minister meets the wishes of the great majority of the members of this house. 1 think we all feel the same way about it, and I suggest that he try to work out an amendment which will

provide that if the husband came here twenty years ago the widow may get entitlement.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: May I ask the minister if there are any widows of Canadian veterans drawing pensions or allowances under the act whose husbands did not qualify for and receive the war veterans' allowance?

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: I want to add my protest to those already expressed. I think this is a case of gross discrimination. I do not believe any widow should be penalized because of the death of her husband. I am sure it was not her fault if she could not keep him alive for twenty years, and the chances are that she did not contribute in any way to his death. I believe this matter should be considered more fully, because after all these widows have contributed their share toward the welfare of the country even after the death of their husbands.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext:
There are just two points I desire to mention. First, I should like to thank hon. members for the constructive suggestions that were made, and I shall attempt to deal with them later. There are two points I want to make with regard to what has been said latterly. First, in response to a direct question asked by the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I may say there is nothing equivalent to the burnt-out pension or war veterans' allowance granted by the British government to Canadians resident in England.

speechtext: That is not what was asked. The member asked about pensions.

subtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER
subsubtopic: MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIAN
speechtext: I understood he was speaking about pensions. The other point regarding widows, I am not going to discuss at length. The basis of this whole legislation is that it is for veterans. It is for that reason we have taken it that twenty years' residence in Canada would bring benefits to these veterans and their dependents equal to those who had served in the Canadian forces, and who are now in receipt of a war veterans' allowance.
